extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, printers, and publishers (esp. academic press staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions for typographical style, punctuation, capitalization, italics, and related composition practices intended to govern the appearance and copy-preparation of publications issued by an academic press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper nouns and adjectives derived from them should be capitalized (examples: George, America, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (to boycott, to pasteurize). Also do not capitalize certain common words used as electrical units (volt, ampere, watt, henry, ohm). Examples and exceptions are given throughout the manual; when in doubt follow the origin/usage and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of name particles (French, Dutch, German)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when to capitalize particles in personal and family names (le, la, de, du, von, van, ten, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally do not capitalize French particles (le, la, de, du) when preceded by a Christian name or title (Miguel de la Torre) but capitalize them when not (La Rochelle). Always capitalize Dutch 'Van' and 'Ten'; never capitalize German 'von'. Personal preference and historical usage account for some exceptions (e.g., Henry van Dyke). Examples are provided for correct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize generic terms that form part of geographical names; do not capitalize when descriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic geographical terms that are integral to a place name are capitalized (Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi River); generic descriptors added as description are not (the river Elbe, the island of Madagascar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual supplies lists of common geographical generic terms and guidance on singular/plural and position relative to the specific name (capitalize Bay, Cape, Lake, Mount, River in appropriate contexts). Consider whether the generic term is an organic part of the proper name or merely descriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize region names and group-designating adjectives only when denoting definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives and nouns used to distinguish definite regions (Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole) are capitalized; ordinary directional words are not when used generically (oriental customs, the southern states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'the North' or 'the East' when used as accepted names for regions; do not capitalize adjectival derivatives in general use (northern Europe). Use judgment about whether a term denotes a recognized region versus a direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of political division terms when part of official names
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic political-division words are capitalized when they are an organic part of an official name (Holy Roman Empire, United Kingdom) or when used singly as an accepted designation (the Union, the States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when they stand alone in a paraphrastic or incomplete designation ('the empire', 'the legislature'). When 'of' introduces an integral part of a name for minor U.S. subdivisions (Department of the Lakes) it is capitalized as part of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, buildings, etc.; generic building types remain lowercase alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, and buildings are capitalized (Drexel Avenue; Lincoln Park; Lakeside Building). Generic building types like 'courthouse', 'post-office', 'library' are not capitalized unless used with an associated place name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize as part of the formal name; when the generic noun is used alone or descriptively, leave lowercase (the courthouse, the library). Exceptions for usage and ambiguity are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of political parties, religious denominations, philosophical/literary/artistic schools and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names of parties, denominations, movements, schools, and their adherents are capitalized (Republican, Catholic, Romantic, Theosophist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the term is used in a general or adjectival sense (republican form of government, pharisaic superciliousness) it is not capitalized. The manual gives many examples distinguishing organization/name usage from general sense usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of monastic orders and members (Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit) are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as proper names; context determines whether a derived adjective or general reference should be lowercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of official and honorific titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Official titles and titles of honor preceding a specific name are capitalized (Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Dr. Davis); abbreviated academic and honorific initials (Ph.D., M.P.) are set without spaces and capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the official title when it follows the name (McKinley, president of the United States) or when used generically or preceded by the article 'the' (the emperor, the senator) except to avoid ambiguity or as established usage. Use small caps and spacing conventions for certain formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of ordinal designations in historical/regimental contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinals indicating dynasties, sessions of Congress, regiments, etc., are capitalized (Eighteenth Dynasty, Fifty-third Congress, Second Illinois Regiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as formal names in listings and citations; minor subdivisions of publications (sec. 4, scene 1) remain lowercased/abbreviated in normal running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of historical epochs, geological ages, and named events
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly accepted epoch and period names and named events are capitalized (Renaissance, Middle Ages, Pleistocene; Thirty Years’ War, Battle of Gettysburg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'age' is capitalized where failure to do so would produce ambiguity (Stone age vs. Middle Ages). Use capitalization to convey conventional epochal names and well‑known event names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of conventions, treaties, creeds, civic and ecclesiastical days
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of notable conventions, treaties, creeds, acts of law, and civic/religious holidays are capitalized (Council of Nicaea, Treaty of Verdun, Apostles' Creed, Fourth of July).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring generically to types of these items rather than specific titled instances, use lowercase (a treaty, the creed). Specific articles and amendment names are capitalized as titled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize principal words in English titles of publications and section headings
rubrics_metrics.description: In English titles (books, pamphlets, periodicals, chapters, articles), capitalize all principal words — nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, first and last words; avoid cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are language-specific exceptions: in Latin capitalize proper nouns and derived adjectives; in French/Italian/Spanish/Scandinavian capitalize only the first word and proper nouns; in German/Danish capitalize all nouns. The Botanical Gazette and similar bibliographic lists may adopt different practices (capitalize only first word and proper names). Hyphenated compounds: capitalize nouns within them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of italics for emphasis, foreign words, and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases for emphasis; foreign words or phrases not fully anglicized; and titles of publications (books, pamphlets, periodicals, long poems printed separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of institutions/places whose English usage requires roman type (Pére Lagrange, Champs Elysées). Avoid excessive italics in bibliographies, tables, or where undue italics would result. The manual lists many foreign words and expressions normally set in italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize words sufficiently anglicized or certain institutional names
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words that have become anglicized or institutional/place names commonly used in English are not italicized (Pére Lagrange is an exception because it is a name; 'the German Reichstag' is roman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider frequency of English usage and presence of English equivalents. Single-sentence foreign passages may be set in reduced type instead of italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize the first word of sentences, poetry lines, and certain other initial positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence and (in prose presentation of poetry) the first word of each line, with special rules for Greek and Latin poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when it introduces an independent sentence or complete passage; do not capitalize short dependent phrases after a colon. Capitalize the first word of a cited speech in direct discourse. In enumerated lists, capitalization depends on whether each item is a complete sentence or independent clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small capitals and small caps usage for formal letter elements and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals and small capitals for town and state in the dateline, salutatory phrase in letters (MY DEAR MR. SMITH:), signatures, and certain formal headings (WHEREAS, SECTION).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set these elements in caps and small caps with prescribed indentation and type-size relationships; the date line and address lines have particular alignment and type-size suggestions. Use 'SECTION' or 'WHEREAS' in caps in constitutions/resolutions per convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lowercase (small initial) for certain common derivatives, subdivisions, and units
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lowercase for common words derived from proper names where the origin is obscured (utopia, bohemian); minor subdivisions in literary references (chapter, section, p., art.); and for units of measurement (lb., oz., yd.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italic side-heads: capitalize only the first word and proper names; the manual lists common abbreviations to be set lowercase and gives examples of when to use lower-case initial letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules for scientific (Latin) names
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, zoological, geological, and paleontological contexts, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera, but not English derivatives; species names capitalization varies by field (botanical/zoological species may be capitalized when derived from names, but geological and medical species names are not capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felidae (capitalized), but 'felids' (lowercase); Felis leo vs. felis (as common). Consult the field-specific instructions for species-level usage and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of names referring to deity and personified abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words used to designate the Supreme Being or Power (the Almighty, Providence, Father, Son, Holy Ghost) and pronouns referring to the same, except in cases where the reference is closely preceded/followed by a distinctive name or the meaning is clear without capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derived or adjectival forms (messianic, messiahship is lowercase). Personified abstract terms (Nature) may be capitalized when personified in the text. Use capitalization sparingly for rhetorical emphasis or to mark contrast (e.g., Church vs. church in antithesis).
